articles.title: Stolen from an Arizona museum in 1985, Willem de Kooning’s painting hung behind a New Mexico bedroom door until antique dealers spotted it in 2017
articles.summary: In a stunning recovery, Willem de Kooning's stolen painting, \"Woman-Ochre,\" was discovered behind a bedroom door in New Mexico, 32 years after its theft from an Arizona museum.
articles.body: Have you ever tried cleaning out a closet and found something that made your jaw drop? Something similar happened to three antique dealers in New Mexico, but it was much bigger than any closet find. The University of Arizona News reported that Willem de Kooning’s painting “Woman-Ochre” was stolen from an Arizona museum in 1985. In 2017, antique dealers found it hanging in a secluded spot behind a bedroom door in a rural New Mexico home. The painting had been missing for over 30 years.A quiet heist on the day after ThanksgivingThe theft took place back in 1985 on the day following Thanksgiving. A man and a woman entered the University of Arizona Museum of Art upon its opening. The woman struck up a conversation with some of the staff as her companion went upstairs to one of the galleries. This room held the work, “Woman-Ochre,” an oil painting by the Dutch American artist Willem de Kooning. The painting had been donated to the university in 1958. The man cut the painting from its frame, rolled it and walked out of the door. By the time security realised that the painting was missing, the duo was long gone. For many years, the only information the FBI had about the robbers was a sketch and the description of a rust coloured sports car.The dealers who spotted itThen in 2017, David Van Auker, Buck Burns and Rick Johnson bought the estate of a woman in rural New Mexico. The three owned Manzanita Ridge, a furniture and antiques store in Silver City. Among the items was a painting that was hanging in an unobtrusive place behind the bedroom door. They took it back to the shop, not thinking much about it until customers began to ask if it was a real de Kooning. Van Auker searched online and found a 2015 Arizona Republic story about the 30th anniversary of the theft, which included a painting that closely resembled his. He called the museum, and exhibitions curator Olivia Miller asked him to send photos. Staff drove for three hours to see it, and three days later the painting was riding back to Tucson in a minivan. A two-hour inspection on campus confirmed that it was real.Repairing the damage at Getty Getting the painting was only half the job. The Getty’s conservation project page states that the painting was recovered 32 years after its theft. However, it was quite badly damaged. The university adds that the painting was torn off from the back, rolled up and then re-stretched and reframed. In 2019, the institution sent the painting to the J. Paul Getty Museum in Los Angeles, where the museum offered to restore it for free. The conservator removed the varnish, stabilised the flaking paint, restored the lost paint, and reattached the canvas to the edges that remained in the original frame. The pandemic slowed down the work at times, but Getty conservators also learned new things about materials and techniques de Kooning used.Home again, but one mystery remains The restored painting was exhibited at the Getty from June to August 2022. It then returned to Tucson in an 18-wheeler with a Homeland Security escort on the night of September 14 and went on exhibit on October 8. Miller said the movement brought relief and peace of mind. Who took it is still officially unknown. The university says suspicion has largely fallen upon the late Jerry and Rita Alter, a couple who owned the home where the painting was found. However, no one has been officially identified as the thief. Museum staff say the ending could have been quite different had the painting been found by someone else. articles.title: Democrat Amy Acton wins Ohio governor race, defeating Vivek Ramaswamy
articles.summary: The raced heated up in its final weeks after the Republican contender released an ad featuring Acton's mother.
articles.body:
Democrat Amy Acton has defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy to win the Ohio governorship in a bitterly contested race, according to CBS News projections.

With this victory, Acton becomes the first Democrat and the first ever woman to win the Ohio governor's race in two decades.

Ohio, a key battleground for much of the 2000s, has voted for Republican Donald Trump in the last three presidential elections, including by 11 points in 2024.

But the gubernatorial race, where voter frustration over the economy and the cost of living was the central theme, took an unexpected turn after the Ramaswamy campaign released a deeply personal attack ad featuring Acton's estranged mother.

In the ad, Acton's mother Donna Arthur said her daughter "lied her entire life". It did not mention that Arthur's husband was charged with raping Acton when she was a child.

The controversial ad loomed over the last weeks of the race. It was criticised by former South Carolina Governor Republican Nikki Haley, while Ohio's current Republican Governor Mike DeWine called it "deeply troubling".

However, some defended it, including President Trump and Vice-President Vance.

Trump described it as "powerful" and encouraged Ramaswamy to keep it running, while Vance, the state's former Senator, said he would like fellow Republicans to stop "whining" about the ad and that he was "a little bit disgusted" by criticism from members of his own party.

Ramaswamy said his campaign would spend $4m (£3m) to air the ad across the state.

After the ad began airing, the editorial board of local Ohio news outlet the Columbus Dispatch endorsed Acton, describing the ad as "revolting and unsettling".

The billionaire biotech entrepreneur ran against Trump for the Republican nomination in 2024. He switched gears to the Ohio governor's race and pitched himself as a political outsider - like Trump - who wanted to develop the president's "America First" agenda.

In his concession speech, Ramaswamy said he is "rooting" for the state, as well as Acton.

Acton is a physician and public health official who talked about her experience with homelessness as a child while campaigning for affordability.

In her acceptance speech on Tuesday, she said "the healing begins today".

"My promise to Ohio, to those who voted for me and those who did not, is that I will work with anyone and everyone, and I always have to make life better for Ohioans," she said.

Acton succeeds Republican Governor Mike DeWine, who is term limited.

Ohio is a swing state that voted for Trump in the 2024 election, but now Republican candidates are facing close challenges across the country.

articles.title: First since 1988: Democrat James Talarico breaks Republican stronghold in Texas
articles.summary: Democrat James Talarico has pulled off a historic victory in Texas, defeating Republican Ken Paxton to end nearly four decades of Republican dominance in
articles.body: Democrat James Talarico has pulled off a historic victory in Texas, defeating Republican Ken Paxton to end nearly four decades of Republican dominance in the state's US Senate elections and deliver a major blow to President Donald Trump. The 37-year-old state legislator's victory marks the first time a Democrat has won a Texas Senate election since 1988, when Lloyd Bentsen secured his final re-election to the chamber.The result is a stunning breakthrough for Democrats in a state Trump carried by double digits just two years ago. Talarico's win also marks a rejection of Trump's decision to back Paxton over incumbent Senator John Cornyn during a bitter Republican primary, despite warnings from party leaders that the former attorney general's baggage could put the seat at risk.Talarico, a former middle school teacher and Presbyterian seminary student, built his campaign around an economic populist message, focusing on the rising cost of living, political corruption and the influence of wealthy donors. Rather than leaning heavily into partisan attacks or divisive culture-war issues, he sought to appeal to independent and disillusioned Republican voters.His central argument was that the country's biggest divide was not between the political left and right, but between the wealthy and ordinary Americans. He repeatedly accused billionaires of using their money to shape politics while arguing that powerful interests had left working families struggling with rising prices.Paxton's record provided another opening. The Republican had spent years weathering legal and personal controversies, including a federal corruption investigation, allegations of abusing his office to benefit a political donor and a securities fraud indictment. Although he was acquitted following an impeachment trial in the Texas Senate and federal prosecutors ultimately brought no charges in the corruption investigation, the controversies remained a central feature of the campaign.Trump had backed Paxton despite concerns among Senate Republicans that his nomination could jeopardise an otherwise winnable seat. The president repeatedly urged voters to treat the midterm elections as a referendum on his leadership, only to distance himself from the results as the losses mounted."I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" Trump wrote on social media on Tuesday night.Talarico's victory was part of a wider Democratic breakthrough in Texas, where Gina Hinojosa also defeated Republican incumbent Greg Abbott to become the state's first Democratic governor since Ann Richards left office in 1995. Hinojosa's victory further underlined the scale of the political shift in a state long considered a Republican stronghold.A former public school teacher, Talarico first entered the Texas House of Representatives in 2018. His legislative work has included reforms to school funding, measures to improve access to mental health programmes and legislation capping insulin co-payments at $25 a month.For Democrats, the victory could offer a blueprint for competing in traditionally Republican territory. For the GOP, losing Texas, a state central to its electoral ambitions, represents a particularly alarming warning ahead of the 2028 presidential race.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2010, a Briton paid about $5 at a Las Vegas garage sale for sketches; one was appraised at up to $2.4 million as a possible Warhol, the authentication board declined to verify it, and it later appeared on eBay for $2 million
articles.summary: Discover the astonishing story of British businessman Alan Fields, who bought a sketch at a Las Vegas garage sale for just $5, only to claim it could be an early Andy Warhol worth $2.4 million. Explore the authentication struggles and the eccentric world of art valuation.
articles.body: Most garage sales tables hold chipped mugs and old paperbacks. In 2010, British businessman Alan Fields said he paid $5 at one in Las Vegas for a handful of framed sketches, ABC News reported in 2012. He later concluded that one of them was an early Andy Warhol drawing, potentially worth millions. The authentication board might once have ruled on it and announced its closure in 2011.Five dollars and a signatureFields once told ABC News that the drawing cost him $5 and that he noticed the signature only while framing it at home. The drawing depicts the singer, Rudy Vallee, set against a background of brightly coloured one-inch squares. Fields said he was told it dates from when Warhol was 11 and ITV News reported that he believes Warhol drew it as a schoolboy in Pittsburgh. According to the Daily Caller, Fields claims the piece pushes the origin of pop art back by almost two decades, since pop art is believed to have started when Warhol was 30. Sources diverge on the origins. ABC News, in an article in 2012, reported that the piece belonged to an aunt of the seller, who had taken care of Warhol during his childhood. According to Fields, in 2013, ABC News reported that the artist grew up within a few blocks of the seller.A $2.4 million valuation Fields told ABC News that Brett Maly, an appraiser from the Art Encounter dealership in Las Vegas, valued the drawing at $2.4 million. In a report by the Las Vegas Review Journal, Maly’s valuation range was given as $1.4 million to $2.39 million. Anyway, this amount puts a value on the drawing as though it were real. This is an appraisal and not a selling price for the piece of artwork. Fields told ABC News in 2013 that he had spent two years trying to authenticate the work.The board that did not authenticate itThe drawing was submitted to the Art Authentication Board of Andy Warhol. According to him, it was returned with a note saying there was not enough evidence and the board was dissolved in October 2011, ABC noted. The press release from the foundation dated 19 October 2011 stated that the board would respond to all requests made before that day and would not accept new requests.PBS Antiques Roadshow explains the backstory. The board had reviewed about 6000 pieces in 15 years, but the board closed down after spending $7 million in a span of three years in its legal battle against collector Joe Simon-Whelan after refusing to authenticate his Warhol portrait. The board was operating on an annual budget of about $500,000 and Mike Strauss, who is the chairman of the foundation, stated in The Wall Street Journal that the money should go to artists and not the lawyer.It meant that it closed down one way of authentication, not all ways. According to PBS, Warhol can still be authenticated by experts and from the foundation catalogue raisonne and according to Meredith Hilferty, who is an appraiser for PBS, nothing much could be done towards selling a Warhol piece if it is omitted from the catalogue. According to ABC, no one person or organisation was authorised to authenticate Warhol pieces by the foundation. This particular article from PBS explains why authentication was hard for Warhol pieces. Warhol had left behind thousands of pieces and many of those pieces were partly produced by assistants working for him at his studio, The Factory.Fields claimed that auction houses did not accept the drawing without authentication. Instead, in August 2013, he put the drawing up for sale through the eBay UK site at a price of $2 million and ABC New claimed that by the end of that Thursday, there were no serious bidders on the drawing.Questions about the family connection and the signatureAccording to the same report by ITV, Fields managed to contact James Warhol, Warhol’s nephew, who claimed that the drawing was not a genuine one. The drawing is signed “Andy Warhol” but HuffPost points out that the artist didn’t drop the final “a” from the Warhola until 1949, roughly a decade after the date Fields gives for the drawing. Thus, the $2 million evaluation of the drawing is based on the owners' assessment, conditional appraisal and a questionable dating of the signature. There has been no authentication done by any authentication board regarding the drawing and the foundation claims that there is currently no one authorised to do it.You use AI every day. articles.title: James Talarico becomes first Democrat to win Texas Senate seat in decades
articles.summary: "This wasn't just a tsunami, not just a referendum, but this was a bloodbath," one expert told the BBC on Democrats' historic wins in Texas.
articles.body:
Democrat James Talarico has won a key Senate race in Texas, in what is likely the single biggest upset for Republicans in this year's elections.

Talarico's stunning victory over Republican Ken Paxton marks the first time a Democrat has won a US Senate seat in Texas since 1988 - and has helped solidify Democrats taking full control of the US Congress in a tidal wave of wins across America.

Talarico, a former schoolteacher, was a little-known figure until last year. He made the rising cost of living under Republican leadership a central theme of his run.

Paxton sought to portray Talarico's views as too progressive for the state, and campaigned alongside Trump on several occasions.

Supporters of Talarico went berserk as TVs at a watch party in Austin, the state's capitol, projected him the winner.

They hugged, they kissed, and they drank to a reality that many say they dared not believe would come true.

Emerging on stage to rapturous applause at his official watch party at a nearby performing arts theatre, Talarico pronounced: "We just took back Texas."

"We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas," he continued, referring to his win over Paxton whose campaign was backed by Elon Musk, the world's richest man.

He invoked religious themes that have grown familiar to his campaign, comparing his unlikely odds to the biblical story of David and Goliath.

"This win, this win is for every Texan who's ever wondered if anyone is listening," he said. "I hear you, we hear you. And tonight the world hears you."

For decades, the idea of a Democrat winning a statewide race had felt like a pipe dream for Texas liberals .

As the nation's second most populous state, Texas has been a bastion of conservatism, routinely rolling out Republican policies that are later employed elsewhere.

But throughout the campaign, polls suggested state legislator Talarico was breaking through with voters, energising a Texas Democratic base desperate for new leadership.

Spending in the race skyrocketed, and it quickly grew to become the most expensive US Senate race in history, with more than half a billion dollars spent.

Billionaire Elon Musk poured in $158m (£117m) to a super PAC supporting Paxton's campaign - a point that Talarico used in attacks on Paxton's campaign.

Then two members of the Bush family , the Republican political dynasty that counts Texas as its political launchpad, backed Talarico in a stunning move foreshadowing Paxton's doom.

George Washington University political science professor Quardricos Driskell told the BBC that Paxton was a major part of Republicans' downfall, calling him an "objectively terrible candidate".

He said the win in Texas by Talarico, combined with another upset on Tuesday that ousted the state's Republican governor Greg Abbott, was "absolutely historic". Abbott's loss marked the first time a Democrat had won a race for governor in the state since the 1990s.

"This wasn't just a tsunami, not just a referendum, but this was a bloodbath," Driskell said about Democrats gains in the Lone Star State. "A clear distinction that the country wants to go in a different direction".

Talarico defeated a well-known opponent, Dallas Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett, in the Democratic primary. Then continued to maintain good polling numbers despite an onslaught of negative adverts, including attacks on past comments where he supported transgender people.

Throughout his campaign, he frequently leaned into his religious upbringing – as the grandson of a Southern Baptist preacher who spent time in a seminary – sprinkling his stump speeches with biblical references.

Paxton had been beleaguered by a number of political scandals, including his impeachment by his own party in 2023 on corruption accusations, before he was later acquitted by the state's Senate.

He was also indicted by the US Securities and Exchange Commission on federal fraud charges, but they were later dismissed.

Trump made multiple stops in Texas to beef up support for Paxton and other Republicans - including in reliably-Republican spots, signalling how concerned party leadership was about turnout.

Voters have been frustrated with high consumer costs, including the price of petrol, and largely blame Trump's tariff policies and the Iran war.

Hispanic voters and those who live along the southern US border have also taken issue with Trump's immigration policies.

Despite border crossings plummeting under Trump - something that had been popular with Texas voters - polls suggested Trump's support among Hispanics, who make up a third of the state's population, had ebbed significantly.

Surveys taken since late summer indicated a majority of Texan Hispanic voters - many of whom switched to Trump to help him win the White House in 2024 - now disapproved of the president. They also suggested that Hispanic voters were favouring Democrats over Republicans by a significant margin.

Many Texas Hispanics who spoke to the BBC before the election pointed to Trump's immigration crackdown as the reasoning behind their change of heart. They pointed to aggressive measures that led to citizens being detained and non-violent offenders being rounded up indiscriminately.

articles.summary: Apple has expanded its warnings about the risks of artificial intelligence, cautioning that autonomous AI agents could access systems without
articles.body: Apple has expanded its warnings about the risks of artificial intelligence, cautioning that autonomous AI agents could access systems without authorisation, send communications, execute transactions and behave in unpredictable ways that may threaten businesses and users, as reported by Fortune. The warning was included in the iPhone maker's latest annual 10-K filing, released a day after the company reported its fourth-quarter financial results. It said AI agents and similar technologies can act on their own: interacting with internal or external systems they may not be authorised to access, executing or altering code, sending communications and completing transactions. Such tools, Apple said, may behave in unintended or unpredictable ways. That includes taking actions nobody directed or authorised, exceeding permissions, or defying and resisting instructions. The company also said rogue agents could conceal their actions, withhold or manipulate information, or generate inaccurate or deceptive outputs.Apple highlights risks from autonomous AI agentsIn the risk factors section of its annual filing, Apple said AI agents and similar technologies are capable of taking actions independently, including interacting with internal and external systems, executing or altering code, sending communications and completing transactions. The company warned that such systems may sometimes attempt to access platforms or services they are not authorised to use. Apple said these technologies could "behave in unintended or unpredictable ways," including taking actions that were not directed, instructed or authorised. The company also warned that AI systems could exceed permissions, ignore instructions or act in ways that differ from their intended purpose.Warning includes concerns about hidden or manipulated informationThe company raised concerns that rogue AI agents could conceal their activities or manipulate information. According to Apple, autonomous AI systems may "conceal actions, hide, withhold or manipulate information, or generate inaccurate or deceptive outputs."The expanded disclosure reflects growing concern across the technology industry about agentic AI systems, which are designed to work more independently and carry out complex tasks on behalf of users.Part of a wider patternApple is not the first big tech company to flag the risk. Alphabet recently raised similar concerns in its own filing, and went further. It said it had seen unexpected behaviour during AI model testing, including agents acting outside their intended scope, which it warned could lead to “severe or catastrophic” security and societal incidents. Fortune noted that these warnings follow several major AI-related security incidents, most notably an attack on Hugging Face by OpenAI agents this summer. Anthropic’s IPO prospectus, made public last week, also lists cases where its models gained unauthorised access to real-world systems during security testing.Microsoft has announced controls to detect, monitor and restrict AI agents, including cutting their permissions or stopping them if they act suspiciously. CEO Satya Nadella has argued that companies should treat agents as potential insider risks and build security controls outside the AI model.AI investments drive costs higherBeyond AI safety concerns, Apple's filing also highlighted challenges related to its AI ambitions. The company said growing demand for cloud computing, storage and AI infrastructure is creating supply constraints, longer lead times and rising costs. Apple noted that shortages of memory and storage components are expected to intensify and could affect its AI rollout plans. The company added that research and development spending rose 32% year-over-year, driven in part by higher infrastructure costs and continued AI investments.Apple CEO John Ternus stresses user awareness and privacySpeaking after the company’s earnings announcement, CEO John Ternus explained that the agentic AI capabilities as promising tools for users but stressed that people must completely understand the access and permissions they grant such systems. Trenus also pointed out the Apple’s ocus on security and privacy as it continues developing AI-powered features and services.The warning underscores a broader shift across the technology sector as companies race to deploy increasingly capable AI agents while simultaneously acknowledging the security, privacy and operational risks that can emerge when autonomous systems gain greater access to data, software and real-world actions.You use AI every day. articles.title: National Trust to 'maintain spirit' of Flatford Wildlife Garden
articles.summary: Flatford Wildlife Garden is bought by the National Trust after being run by the RSPB for 15 years.
articles.body:
The National Trust has vowed to "maintain the spirit" of a nature reserve while making "some small changes" after saving it from closure.

The future of Flatford Wildlife Garden, near East Bergholt in Suffolk, was thrown into doubt in October when the RSPB said it would have to sell or lease the land due to financial pressures.

It was announced in April that the site would be taken on by the National Trust and, on Tuesday, ownership of the garden officially changed hands.

RSPB Suffolk area manager Adam Rowlands said: "We are confident that their ambitions for the site align with our own ethos of how we wanted to see Flatford Wildlife Garden looked after under new ownership."

He added: "We know the National Trust will continue to maintain the garden for both wildlife and people, and we are incredibly pleased it will reopen to the public next year under their care."

Leigh Freeman, a National Trust area manager, said the purchase had been a "quite a long time in the making" for both parties and would help secure the future of the reserve, a legacy left to the RSPB by Sylvia and Margaret Richardson about 15 years ago.

"The RSPB had a look at its assets last year and I think it felt more aligned that we would look after it in the future," he said.

"It's only been open in the summer in the past, but we will be taking the winter to kind of get it ready for visitors in the spring – early March or certainly before Easter."

The gardens, which have been managed by the RSPB since 2011, boast wildlife and birds, a trail with carved wooden garden creatures and a pond.

There is also a living willow tunnel and an insect and bee "hotel" and there are activity days and talks for children and adults.

The acquisition, which also includes land next to the gardens, was made possible after the National Trust, a conservation charity that cares for historic buildings, gardens and landscapes, received support and funding from local groups.

Freeman said the first year of ownership would be spent learning more about the garden and how it "integrates with the site and people connect with it".

"There will be some small changes but we intend to maintain the spirit of the wildlife garden, that is something we are very committed to," added Freeman.

"We're also really committed to connecting it with the wider site at Flatford and providing better access."

articles.title: Kent restored rocking horses bring back childhood memories
articles.summary: Marc and Tony Stevenson say people are often moved to tears when reunited with childhood favourites.
articles.body:
The twin brothers behind a company making rocking horses in Kent have said they keep a tissue box to hand as customers get emotional about recapturing their childhoods.

Marc Stevenson and Tony Stevenson, founders of Stevenson Brothers Rocking Horses, both recently turned 70, having established the company on their 26th birthdays in 1982.

"It's such an emotional thing to be involved in," said Marc.

Based in a workshop in Bethersden, near Ashford, the company has created bespoke rocking horses for customers around the world and restored antique models for families wanting to preserve childhood memories.

The brothers have also created rocking horses modelled on real horses, including Magna Carta and Barbers Shop, both racehorses owned by Queen Elizabeth II.

Tony said they restore a lot of old rocking horses for customers.

"People love it because that's how they remember seeing it and then, 30 years later, it's all worn out and everything. We put it back to the way it used to be."

Marc added that customers often become tearful when they come in and see their horse as it takes them back to being a child.

"Boom - out comes the tissue box," he said.

"Well, actually I cry a lot too with people. It's such an emotional thing to be involved in."

"I mean we're making pieces of art. These are sculptures."

The brothers marked their 70th birthdays last month with a lunch at Boys Hall in Willesborough, where some of the company's earliest promotional photographs were taken after the firm was first set up in 1982.

They still have photographs of the first rocking horses on the lawn.

Tony said it was impossible to be too serious when rocking on a rocking horse, describing it as "a great way to chill out".

Marc said: "It's feeding the inner child so it keeps us young.

"In fact, we call [the] rocking horses, our 'youthing' machines.

"Lots of our clients are grown-up girls and boys who maybe didn't get one when they were little."

Looking ahead to the company's 50th anniversary, he said: "We should be retiring, really, but we love what we do and we're very good at what we do."

articles.title: Similar solar farm plans to boost Berkshire councils' coffers
articles.summary: Neighbouring councils are aiming to generate energy and money by running their own solar farms.
articles.body:
Two neighbouring councils are aiming to generate green energy and money to fund local services by building and running their own large solar farms.

Work begins next week to install 43,000 solar panels on fields that Wokingham Borough Council owns in the village of Barkham .

West Berkshire Council said construction would begin at its site near Grazeley in March, with plans for 35,000 panels.

The schemes are not connected but are just a few miles apart, and are expected to be operational by the end of 2027.

About 20 councils in the country currently own and run solar farms.

Both Liberal Democrat-led authorities have said their plans will contribute towards ambitious targets to cut carbon to net zero by the end of the decade.

Imogen Shepherd-Dubey, Wokingham's executive member for finance and governance, said the authority had a duty to ensure its assets were creating the best value for the public.

She said: "This is something new. We own this land, we might as well make the best of it.

"It will generate electricity that will help us run all of our council services, help us run our schools and libraries and public facilities, and what we don't use we will sell back to the grid.

"Because of the financial pressures that councils are under, they are having to look more laterally at how they use public money, and this is one of the examples.

"The margins on this seem quite high, it is speculative, but everything looks very good.

"Any investment has an element of risk, but I'm feeling the risks on this are very, very low."

Listen to the latest news from Berkshire

Wokingham's solar farm has been costed at £24m and is expected to turn a profit of more than £1m annually across a 40-year lifespan before it is restored to farmland.

The generating potential of some privately-run solar farms has been hampered by a backlog and delays in making firm connections to the National Grid .

But with an existing substation nearby, the facility should be operational from next September, with full connection completed in 2029, following a government order to reprioritise schemes that are ready-to-go.

West Berkshire's solar farm will cost £18.6m to build, and is projected to make £10m profit over its 40-year lifespan.

Council leader Jeff Brooks said it would make a dramatic impact on the council's carbon footprint.

"The business case stood up to scrutiny," he told the BBC.

"We're moving towards net zero in our own council usage, of electricity and energy. This will take us a big step forward on it, so it's exciting.

"Rather than a leap of faith, all the technical impact of it has all been considered. It will be up and running pretty quickly, so what's not to like really?"

The council inherited the land 30 years ago, and it has been run by a tenant farmer since. Three of its large fields will be given over to power generation.

Brooks said it was pure coincidence that both councils were working on similar schemes.

"We were aware, but they're not linked," he explained.

"I think we've both got it right. Councils are risk averse, they take a precautionary principle, but I'm from a business background that says if a business case stands up, go for it.

"All councils should be looking at how they generate new money, and that new money can come from enterprises like the things we're doing here.

"So you don't rely just on on council tax, or government grants, which are going down all the time. You look to see where's those new streams of income. This is one."

articles.title: Sightings of Asian hornet nests in Guernsey double in a year
articles.summary: The nests are treated so populations of the insect are kept "as low as possible", experts say.
articles.body:
More than 30 Asian hornet nests have been found in Guernsey this season, doubling the number discovered in 2025, according to spotters.

Asian hornets are an invasive species and an aggressive predator of many types of insect, especially honey bees.

Despite the rise in sightings, the States of Guernsey said it continued to tackle the issue by "actively tracking" hornets back to their nests which are then treated with a powder-based pesticide.

Annelotte Daas-Jehan, invasive non-native species policy and co-ordination officer for the States, said: "I am surprised but not shocked because we know what's happening in other islands and many other European countries."

She added: "It is definitely concerning we are seeing an increase in the amount of hornet nests.

"But if we look on the positive side, that we have found so many and were able to treat so many means we can keep the population as low as possible."

Figures shared by the States showed a total of 44 nests were discovered from March 2026 up to now - including one nest found damaged after Storm Austen.

Seventeen nests were identified in the year up to December 2025, according to the figures.

The figures, which include both primary and secondary nests, compared with four found 2024, 19 in 2023 and four in 2022. Asian hornets were first detected in Guernsey in 2017.

Primary nests housing up to 100 insects are built by queens at the start of the season to raise a set of workers, Daas-Jehan said.

The queen then seeks a secondary location, potentially high up in a tree, or by expanding the existing nest to create a "secondary nest", which can contain up to 5,000 insects, she said.

She said nests create the greatest public health risk when they are at sites most likely to be disturbed by people such as in brambles, hedges or roof spaces.

The States said Asian hornets also posed a major threat to the island's biodiversity, with 39% of the hornets' diet being honey bees.

Daas-Jehan, who has been in post since April, said there had been a "rapid increase" in Asian hornet popuations across Europe with "pressure increasing" on authorities to act.

She said their strategy was to "flatten the curve" of the increase through a strategy of killing queens and managing nests, which she said was "doable".

"I hope that happens this year," she said.

Daas-Jehan said they were tracking queens in the spring when they come out of hibernation to look for sugar resources and "taking out" the queen could then prevent her from building a full colony.

She asked that people continue to report nest and wasp sightings to help curb the increase.

"At this time of year hornets are being spotted on flowering Fatsia japonica and camellias so if you have either of these plants in your garden or nearby please keep an eye out," she said.

articles.title: Netanyahu faces coalition showdown as rivals maneuver to form Israel's next government
articles.summary: Benjamin Netanyahu faces a critical test as President Isaac Herzog decides who will receive the mandate to form Israel's next government.
articles.body: TEL AVIV, Israel: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s hold on power in Israel will be tested Wednesday as President Isaac Herzog begins consultations with leaders of all parties elected to the 26th Knesset before deciding which lawmaker to task with forming the next government. The final vote count, published last Friday by Israel's Central Elections Committee, gave Netanyahu's bloc 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared with 48 for the opposition alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot — 61 seats are needed to form a government. On Monday, Netanyahu posted to X that "the public in Israel does not want a government that depends on Ra'am and the Joint List—parties that support terrorism and reject the existence of the Jewish state." NETANYAHU DEFIES EXIT POLLS AS VOTE SHIFTS IN HIS FAVOR, BUT MAJORITY REMAINS ELUSIVE "A clear majority in the Jewish public chose the Likud as the largest party and me, as prime minister, to lead the next government. We aspire to form a broad government with our partners and with any party that wishes to do so and does not support terrorism. I am open to holding discussions on the matter," he added. The two predominantly Arab parties he pointed his criticism at are the Joint List and Ra'am who secured a historic combined total of 19 seats, potentially positioning them as kingmakers in the government formation process. A Joint List source told Fox News Digital that the alliance is likely to endorse Eisenkot to be the first lawmaker tasked with forming a government. If both predominantly Arab parties were to back him, he would receive recommendations from parties representing more than the 61 seats needed. The lawmaker tasked with forming a government will have 28 days to do so, with the president authorized to grant an extension of up to 14 additional days. Consultations will be held in ascending order of seat count, beginning with Religious Zionism-Zehut and Shas, which each won six seats, followed by Yisrael Beiteinu, which secured seven. On Thursday, Herzog will meet with the leaders of United Torah Judaism and Otzma Yehudit, which each won seven seats, followed by The Democrats and Ra'am, which each won eight, the Joint List (11), BeYachad (12), Yashar (21) and Likud (27). Defense and government affairs commentator Amir Oren told Fox News Digital that while Herzog is formally free to choose whom to task with forming a government, he would be inclined to select the candidate whose nomination is backed by parties representing a majority of Knesset seats. FORMER ISRAELI PM EMERGES AS WILD CARD IN HIGH-STAKES ELECTION WITH MIDDLE EAST'S FUTURE AT STAKE "He must then task Eisenkot with forming the next government. That does not mean Eisenkot will succeed. If he fails, he will have to return the mandate to the president," Oren said. Eisenkot may, in fact, struggle to assemble a 61-seat governing coalition, given competing interests within the opposition bloc. BeYachad leader Naftali Bennett and Yisrael Beiteinu chief Avigdor Liberman are unlikely to agree to serve in a government reliant on the Joint List, given the latter’s pro-Palestinian positions and opposition to Zionism. It is theoretically possible, however, that the opposition bloc could agree to form a minority government with the Arab parties providing support from outside the coalition. While Israel has no precedent for forming a minority government immediately following an election, such arrangements have occurred during a Knesset term. Most recently, during Netanyahu’s current term, one of the ultra-Orthodox parties withdrew from the coalition over a dispute related to military conscription but continued to support the government from outside. Religious Zionism-Zehut, Otzma Yehudit and Shas each confirmed to Fox News Digital on Tuesday night that they would recommend Netanyahu to Herzog during consultations on forming a government. Dan Diker, president of the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs, told Fox News Digital that Bennett and Liberman’s recent endorsement of Eisenkot suggests they are moving away from the prospect of a national unity government. "I think it would behoove Netanyahu, Eisenkot, former Prime Minister Bennett and former Defense Minister Liberman to find a way to work together now, given the imminent clash between the apocalyptic death cult known as the Iranian regime, Israel and, by extension, the rest of the Western world," he said. Complicating matters for Netanyahu, the 26th Knesset is scheduled to be sworn in on Nov. 10. Its newly elected members are expected to begin forming committees and advancing legislation, while the current prime minister and ministers remain in office and continue carrying out their duties under the oversight of the new parliament, ensuring continuity of government. WHO IS ITAMAR BEN-GVIR, THE ISRAELI FIREBRAND RISING WITH THE POPULIST RIGHT ACROSS THE GLOBE? "They are doing everything they can to push Netanyahu out of office, and we are seeing that now with discussions about replacing the Knesset speaker. They can then begin trying to advance legislation in a Knesset with 19 seats held by Arab parties that would be very uncomfortable for Netanyahu," Diker said. Oren highlighted another potential challenge, suggesting that the caretaker government's ability to launch military operations could face political constraints, potentially complicating any resumption of hostilities with Iran, even if U.S. President Donald Trump were to initiate such action. Former Knesset member Dov Lipman told Fox News Digital that Eisenkot appears likely to be the first lawmaker tasked with forming a government, but suggested that most Israelis favor a national unity government built around Likud, Yashar and BeYachad, with one or more smaller parties also joining. "As a first step, Eisenkot may approach Likud and ask it to join a government under his leadership, which Likud will reject. Eisenkot will then have to make a decision, as Liberman is unlikely to agree to serve in a government alongside Arab parties," Lipman said. "Eisenkot will likely fail to form a government, after which the mandate will pass to Netanyahu, who will also likely fail." That would trigger a 21-day period during which any Knesset member could attempt to form a government with the backing of at least 61 lawmakers. If the process reaches that stage, Eisenkot might agree to serve under Netanyahu for two years to avoid sending the country to another election, Lipman said. Prof. Gideon Rahat, a senior fellow at the Israel Democracy Institute, told Fox News Digital that Netanyahu would need to make concessions to persuade opposition leaders that he would honor his commitments, given their experience with the 2020 power-sharing agreement with then-Blue and White party leader Benny Gantz. NETANYAHU REVEALS HE WANTS AMERICAN FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL TO 'DRAW DOWN TO ZERO' Under the agreement, Netanyahu was to serve as prime minister for the first 18 months, with Gantz serving as alternate prime minister and defense minister before taking over as premier on Nov. 17, 2021. However, the arrangement unraveled after the government failed to pass a state budget by the December 2020 deadline, triggering the Knesset's automatic dissolution and new elections. Gantz never assumed the premiership. Rahat pointed to Israel’s 1984-1988 national unity government as a precedent, saying a similar arrangement could work. "At the time, Israel was still embroiled in the Lebanon War, with IDF forces deployed in the country, while the economy was facing a severe crisis, with annual inflation exceeding 400%. Against that backdrop, Likud and Labor formed a national unity government under a rotation agreement, with Shimon Peres serving as prime minister for the first two years, followed by Yitzhak Shamir for the next two," he said. While large parts of the public would likely support it, Rahat said, there are still issues that may create tension. But when it comes to major issues of security and the economy, unity governments can be quite effective," Rahat said. "Once they resolve the major challenges, however, they start fighting among themselves and the magic is over."
